sentences.text: JUDGMENT
This is a suit for recovery of 3,03,614/-with pendente lite & future interest and declaration.

The brief facts as stated in the plaint are:
1.

It is stated that the plaintiff is the registered owner of Maruti Alto K-10 bearing RC number DL-12CH-1719 (hereinafter referred to as "the vehicle") and the same was insured with defendant no.1 (erstwhile M/s Bharti Axa General Insurance Co. Ltd) through defendant no.2.

sentences.text: It is stated that the plaintiff paid insurance premium for the period from 22.12.2018 to 21.12.2019 under a comprehensive insurance policy number S7072589.

It is stated that defendant no.2, as an agent of Hardwari Lal vs M/S Bharti Axa General Insurance Co Ltd ... on 13 May, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/175915390/

sentences.text: It is stated that on 13.06.2019, when the son of the plaintiff, namely, Sh. Ashok Kumar was returning home in the vehicle, he met with an accident at Raja Puri Road, Uttam Nagar at about 6:25 am.
It is stated that a dog suddenly came in front of the vehicle and in order to save it, the vehicle struck to thada (shop step) and a broken pole, thereby damaging the vehicle.
3. It is stated that Sh. Ashok Kumar tried contacting the defendants but his call could not be connected.
It is stated that a recovery van from City24 crane service was called and the vehicle was taken to M/s Krishna Automobile Workshop, Sector-10, Dwarka on the same day.
It is stated that a claim form was filled up at the workshop and the workshop informed defendant no.1 telephonically.

4. It is stated that on 15.06.2019, the plaintiff received a call that a surveyor, Sh. Saurabh Saxena,
had inspected the vehicle and taken its photographs.

It is stated that when the plaintiff telephonically contacted the surveyor, he told the plaintiff that his claim was being rejected since his explanation of the accident did not match the damages on the vehicle.
It is stated that the plaintiff tried explaining the facts to the surveyor and also requested him to visit the spot of the accident but he remained adamant to reject the plaintiff's claim.

5. It is stated that after the plaintiff contacted defendant no.2, the surveyor agreed to visit the place of the accident and also demanded photographs of the spot from the plaintiff, but the plaintiff did not have any.

6. It is stated that on 20.07.2019, a letter dated 16.07.2019 was received by the plaintiff wherein the claim of the plaintiff had been rejected on false grounds and he had been notified that further insurance of the vehicle had also been forfeited on account of misrepresentation of facts.
7. It is stated that the plaintiff and his son tried calling defendant no.1 company but they did not listen to them and disconnected their calls.

8. It is stated that when the plaintiff did not get any satisfactory reply, he filed a complaint with IRDA on 24.07.2019 and with defendant no.1.
9.
It is stated that the workshop had assessed the damages and the cost of repairing the vehicle at approximately 1.45 lakhs, which estimate was also provided to the surveyor.
10. It is stated that the plaintiff is an advocate by profession and he used to drive the vehicle to attend different courts and also to visit his native place at Mahendra Garh, Haryana.
It is stated that the son of the plaintiff was also working at Sega Company in Bahadurgarh, Haryana.
It is stated that in the rainy season, the plaintiff suffered a loss by hiring cabs to go to different places.

12. It is stated that the defendants have violated the terms of the policy and hence, the plaintiff served a legal notice dated 14.08.2019 on defendant no.1 and a reminder dated 11.12.2019 but to no avail.

It is also prayed that the letter dated 16.07.2019 issued by defendant no.1 be declared null and void.

It is stated that after cross-checking the documents submitted by the plaintiff and the surveyor, it was found that the accident description mentioned in the claim form did not match the vehicle damages, and the types of damages seem to have been caused due to negligence and carelessness of the plaintiff.
15. It is stated that the plaintiff had filed the claim form on 13.06.2019, whereas he intimated defendant no.1 on 15.06.2019.

It is stated that the plaintiff had misrepresented the facts and not disclosed material information to defendant no.1 at the time of applying for the claim, which is a violation of the terms and conditions of the insurance policy.

16. It is stated that the in-house surveyor of defendant no.1 had inspected the vehicle at M/s Shree Krishna Automobile and he had rightly informed the plaintiff that his claim would be repudiated on account of a mismatch of facts.
17. It is stated that as per the repair assessment processing sheet, the estimated repair cost/final claim amount ascertained by the surveyor was 15,866.90.
It is stated that the declared insured value of the vehicle (IDV) as mentioned on the insurance policy is 1,62,500 and the company cannot pay any amount higher than the IDV of the vehicle.

19. Defendant no.2 did not enter appearance and was proceeded ex parte.

Issue-wise findings are as under:
"Issue no. iv) Whether the claim of the plaintiff was not maintainable due to misrepresentation of facts and non disposal of material information by the plaintiff?
...OPD"
and "Issue no. iii) Whether the plaintiff is entitled for the relief of declaration to declare the letter dated 16.07.2019 as null and void as prayed for? ...OPP"
25.
(There is a typographical error in the issue no. iv as it mentions "disposal" instead of "disclosure".
The error stands rectified under Section 152 CPC.)
Both these issues are interlinked and are, therefore, taken up for adjudication together.

The onus of proving issue no. iv) was on defendant no.1 and the onus of proving issue no. iii) was on the plaintiff.
26.

Defendant no.1 has rejected the claim of the plaintiff on two grounds: one that he did not inform the company immediately after the accident, and two that he misrepresented the facts to the insurance company.
Although this issue is framed only regarding the second ground, I shall deal with both the grounds under this issue.
27. At the outset, it is profitable to note here that none of the parties have filed the insurance policy.
While the plaintiff claims that he never received the insurance policy but only the insurance certificate, defendant no.1 has not given any justification for not filing the insurance policy.
The detailed terms and conditions of the coverage plan offered by the insurer are mentioned in the insurance policy whereas the Certificate of Insurance only proves that the vehicle is insured.

sentences.text:
Section 91 of the Evidence Act provides that when the terms of a contract have been reduced to the form of a document, and in all cases in which any matter is required by law to be reduced to the form of a document, no evidence shall be given in proof of the terms of such contract or of such matter, except the document itself, or secondary evidence of its contents in cases in which secondary evidence is admissible under the provisions hereinbefore contained.
29.

Therefore, before arguing that any act of the plaintiff brought him out of the purview of benefits of the insurance policy, the policy letter ought to have been filed by defendant no.1.
30.

Resultantly, this Court has referred to the terms and conditions of the Certificate of Insurance Ex PW1/3 and Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (Insurance Surveyors And Loss Assessors) Regulations, 2015 (hereinafter referred to as "the Rules") to assess the contentions of the parties.

entities.text: Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (Insurance Surveyors And Loss Assessors) Regulations, 2015
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: 31. There is no stipulation in the certificate Ex PW1/3 as to the period within which an insured must notify the insurance company.
32. Ld Counsel for defendant no.1 has argued that there is a delay in reporting the accident.
It is submitted that the accident took place on 13.06.2019, whereas defendant no.1 was notified about it on 15.06.2019 by the workshop where the vehicle had been taken.
It is stated that delays in reporting the accident hinder the insurer's liability to conduct timely investigations, assess the extent of damages and verify the accuracy of the claim.
It is argued that this delay is a clear violation of the policy's terms and conditions which stipulate immediate notification of any accidents to facilitate a prompt and thorough claims process.
33. I am unable to find much force in this argument because as noted above, this court has not been informed of the terms and conditions of the policy by which the vehicle was governed.

Although,
having regard to the Rules, it is reasonable to assume that there should be prompt reporting of the accident, however, in the absence of any stipulation specifically explaining what would be considered as a 'delay in reporting', it would be unfair to hold the plaintiff/insured liable for the same, particularly when the alleged period of delay is only two days.
34. Ld Counsel for defendant no.1 has placed reliance on the judgment in the case of Gurshinder Singh vs Sriram General Insurance Ltd, AIR 2020 SC 1395 in this regard.

entities.text: Gurshinder Singh vs Sriram General Insurance Ltd, AIR 2020 SC 1395
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In this judgment, the Hon'ble Supreme Court, while interpreting 'Condition No. 1 of Standard Form For Commercial Vehicles Package Policy' observed that the company should be immediately notified in writing by the insured about the accident.

However, in the very same judgment, the Hon'ble Supreme Court observed:
"18.

We concur with the view taken in the case of Om Prakash (supra), that in such a situation if the claimant is denied the claim merely on the ground that there is some delay in intimating the insurance company about the occurrence of the theft, it would be taking a hyper technical view.

We find, that this Court in Om Prakash (supra) has rightly held that it would not be fair and reasonable to reject genuine claims which Hardwari Lal vs M/S Bharti Axa General Insurance Co Ltd ... on 13 May, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/175915390/
6 had already been verified and found to be correct by the investigator.
19.

entities.text: Hardwari Lal vs M/S Bharti Axa General Insurance Co Ltd
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: We find, that this Court in Om Prakash (supra) has rightly held that the Consumer Protection Act aims at protecting the interest of the consumers and it being a beneficial legislation deserves pragmatic construction.

We find, that in Om Prakash(supra) this Court has rightly held that mere delay in intimating the insurance company about the theft of the vehicle should not be a shelter to repudiate the insurance claim which has been otherwise proved to be genuine."
35. In the case of Om Prakash v. Reliance General Insurance and Anr. 2018(1) CPR 907 (SC), a truck had been stolen and there was a delay in giving intimation to the insurance company,

entities.text: Om Prakash v. Reliance General Insurance and Anr. 2018(1) CPR 907 (SC)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
while allowing the appeal, the Hon'ble Supreme Court observed:
"11.
It is common knowledge that a person who lost his vehicle may not straightaway go to the Insurance Company to claim compensation.
At first, he will make efforts to trace the vehicle.
It is true that the owner has to intimate the insurer immediately after the theft of the vehicle.
However, this condition should not bar settlement of genuine claims particularly when the delay in intimation or submission of documents is due to unavoidable circumstances.
The decision of the insurer to reject the claim has to be based on valid grounds.
Rejection of the claims on purely technical grounds in a mechanical manner will result in loss of confidence of policy-holders in the insurance industry.
If the reason for delay in making a claim is satisfactorily explained, such a claim cannot be rejected on the ground of delay.
It is also necessary to state here that it would not be fair and reasonable to reject genuine claims which had already been verified and found to be correct by the Investigator.
The condition regarding the delay shall not be a shelter to repudiate the insurance claims which have been otherwise proved to be genuine.
It needs no emphasis that the Consumer Protection Act aims at providing better protection of the interest of consumers.
It is a beneficial legislation that deserves liberal construction.
This laudable object should not be forgotten while considering the claims made under the Act."

36. It also needs to be emphasised that Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority (in short,
"IRDA") had issued Circular to all life-insurers and non- life insurers dated 20.09.2011 regarding delay in claim intimation/documents submission with respect to all life insurance contracts and all non-life individual and group insurance contracts.

The same is reproduced hereunder:
"CIRCULAR Ref. IRDA/HLTH/MISC/CIR/216/09/2011 Dated:20.09.2011 To: All life insurers and non-life insurers.
Re: Delay in claim intimation/documents submission with respect to i. All life insurance contracts and ii. All Non-life individual and group insurance contracts.
The Authority has been receiving several complaints that claims are being rejected on the ground of delayed submission of intimation and documents.

The current contractual obligation imposing the condition that the claims shall be intimated to the insurer with prescribed documents within a specified number of days is necessary for insurers for effecting various post claim activities like Hardwari Lal vs M/S Bharti Axa General Insurance Co Ltd ... on 13 May, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/175915390/
7 investigation, loss assessment, provisioning, claim settlement etc.

entities.text: Hardwari Lal vs M/S Bharti Axa General Insurance Co Ltd
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: However, this condition should not prevent settlement of genuine claims, particularly when there is delay in intimation or in submission of documents due to unavoidable circumstances.
The insurer's decision to reject a claim shall be based on sound logic and valid grounds.
It may be noted that such limitation clause does not work in isolation and is not absolute.
One needs to see the merits and good spirit of the clause, without compromising on bad claims.
Rejection of claims on purely technical grounds in a mechanical fashion will result in policyholders losing confidence in the insurance industry, giving rise to excessive litigation.
Therefore, it is advised that all insurers need to develop a sound mechanism of their own to handle such claims with utmost care and caution.

It is also advised that the insurers must not repudiate such claims unless and until the reasons of delay are specifically ascertained, recorded and the insurers should satisfy themselves that the delayed claims would have otherwise been rejected even if reported in time.

The insurers are advised to incorporate additional wordings in the policy documents,
suitable enunciating insurers' stand to condone delay on merit for delayed claims where the delay is proved to be for reasons beyond the control of the insured.
Sd/- J. Harinarayan CHAIRMAN."

37. These directions were reiterated in another circular, which is reproduced hereunder:
"CIRCULAR IRDA/NL/CIR/MISC/149/06/2017 Dt: 28th June, 2017 To CEOs/CMDs of All General Insurance Companies, Life Insurance Companies and Health Insurance Companies Re: Delay in Claim Intimation/Documents Submission.

The Authority, vide circular no. IRDA/HLTH/MISC/ CIR/216/09/2011 dated 20.09.2011, issued guidelines as to how to deal with delayed intimation of claims and delayed submission of documents by the claimants.

Since , some insurance companies were not adhering to the provisions of the circular,
the Authority further issued directions under section 34(1) of the Insurance Act, 1938 , vide no.IRDA/NL/MISC/CIR/214/10/2016 dated 28.10.2016 clarifying that the circular dated 20.09.2011 is binding on the insurers.

Recently, in a legal case the Hon'ble High Court, while passing the order made several adverse comments against the Insurance Companies' non-compliance of the Authority's direction and ordered the Authority to take appropriate remedial measures.
In view of the above, you are hereby advised to ensure compliance with the said circulars scrupulously.

Sd/-

38.

The gist of the aforesaid circulars issued by the IRDA and the ratio of the judgments of the Hon'ble Supreme Court is that the condition regarding the delay shall not be a shelter to repudiate the insurance claims, which have been otherwise proved to be genuine.

The decision of the insurer to reject the claim has to be based on valid grounds and rejection of the claims on purely technical grounds in a mechanical manner will result in loss of confidence of policy-holders in the insurance industry.
39. This brings us to the second ground of rejection, that is, the plaintiff has indulged in misrepresentation of facts.
It is argued that the damages claimed by the plaintiff are exaggerated.
It is stated that it was the duty of the plaintiff to prove that the damages claimed were genuinely attributable to the reported accident, but he has failed to do so.

It is stated that the plaintiff/insured had given an undertaking at the time of submission of the claim that he had made a correct and complete statement, and in case of any false/fraudulent statement or suppression/concealment, the policy shall be void.

It is stated that the surveyor had prepared a report and found that the description of the accident did not match the damages on the vehicle and therefore, the insurance of the vehicle stood forfeited.

40. Ld Counsel for defendant no.1 has argued that as per the Insurance Act, a surveyor must be appointed where a claim of more than 20,000 is raised and the plaintiff also had the option to appoint a surveyor but he did not do so.
It is stated that the plaintiff not only failed to inform defendant no.1 but also did not take any photos of the spot where the accident had taken place to support his claim.

41. As far as the appointment of a surveyor by the plaintiff is concerned, no rules of insurance or terms of the insurance contract have been brought to my notice that the plaintiff could appoint his own surveyor or that he was made aware that such a right exists in him.
42. Nevertheless, let us consider the testimony of D1W1-the surveyor of defendant no.1.

Admittedly,
D1W1 had examined the vehicle but he never went to the spot of the accident.
He deposed that he prepared a report dated 16.07.2019 Mark A after the inspection.
This document being a photocopy is not admissible in evidence.

There are some photographs which were purportedly taken by D1W1,
but he neither relied upon such photographs during his testimony nor proved the same by furnishing a certificate under Section 65B of the Evidence Act.
43. He further stated that the reason of repudiation was reflected in another document Mark B.
This document is also a photocopy or a printout, not bearing the signatures of any of the mentioned signatories.
Neither the original nor a certificate under section 65B Evidence Act was furnished for this document also.

44. During his cross-examination, D1W1 stated that he had seen some photographs of the spot on WhatsApp which he relied on instead of visiting the spot, however, such photographs have not been filed by defendant no.1.

Hardwari Lal vs M/S Bharti Axa General Insurance Co Ltd ... on 13 May, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/175915390/
9 45.

entities.text: Hardwari Lal vs M/S Bharti Axa General Insurance Co Ltd
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: D1W1 also stated that it was not his duty to visit the site and enquire about the incident/accident.
46. This argument does not find favour with me.
A car insurance surveyor is assigned the task of assessing the cause and extent of the damage and therefore, he must inspect the damaged car as well as the spot before preparing his report.
One fails to understand how the surveyor could say that the description of the accident did not match the damages when he had not even seen the spot of the accident.
Can one decide the probabilities of the accident only by seeing the vehicle?
And if in peculiar circumstances one can do so, can the surveyor justify his conclusion without giving a detailed explanation?
The answers to both these questions must be negative.

47. As per the Rules, the duties of a surveyor include:
"Rule 13(1)(e)'examining, inquiring, investigating, verifying and checking upon the causes and the circumstances of the loss in question including extent of loss, nature of ownership and insurable interest and (f) conducting spot and final surveys, as and when necessary and comment upon franchise, excess/under insurance and any other related matter"
48.

Clearly, there has been a dereliction of duties by the surveyor of defendant no.1.
49.
Further, D1W2, the legal manager of defendant no.1 has deposed that the accident seems to have been caused due to negligence and carelessness of the plaintiff.
It is difficult to comprehend how such a sweeping and assertive statement can be made in the absence of any eyewitness to the accident and without even conducting an on-site inspection.

50. D1W2 has further testified that the damage caused to the vehicle did not occur due to hitting a dog as the whole front side fender and windscreen of the vehicle were damaged, which reflects the malafide intention of the plaintiff.
51. However, this is contrary to the statement to the claim of the plaintiff.
The plaintiff had never contended that his vehicle had hit the dog.
Rather, it was his case that in order to save the dog, the vehicle had hit the divider (or thada) on one side and a pole on the other side.
It is also explained in the claim that due to the impact of the collision, PW2/Sh. Ashok, who was driving the vehicle had hit his head on the windscreen.

52. The plaintiff has testified that after the accident, he took the vehicle to the workshop where an estimated cost of repairing was given as 1.45 lakhs (estimate is Ex PW1/6), however, when the insurance company refused to pass the claim, he got only the most pressing repairs done at a cost of 52,514.
53.
When the plaintiff got the vehicle examined at the workshop, he had discharged his onus to show that the damages were attributable to the accident.

It was the surveyor's job to dispute the estimated Hardwari Lal vs M/S Bharti Axa General Insurance Co Ltd ... on 13 May, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/175915390/
10 cost provided by the workshop.

entities.text: Hardwari Lal vs M/S Bharti Axa General Insurance Co Ltd
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 54. The plaintiff has testified that he repeatedly tried to contact the surveyor and tried to explain to him the complete facts and even requested him to visit the spot of the accident but the surveyor remained adamant on his stand.

The plaintiff has further proved vide his letter Ex PW1/8 that he had provided the photographs of the spot of the accident and the photographs of the damaged car,
but the surveyor rejected his claim without giving any written information to him.

55. Rule 13(2) of the Rules provides that a surveyor or loss assessor whether appointed by the insurer or the insured, shall submit his report to the insurer as expeditiously as possible with a copy of the report to the insured giving his comments on the insured's consent or otherwise on the assessment of loss.
It is nobody's case that a copy of the report of D1W1 was ever supplied to the plaintiff or his comments were taken on the report.

56. Therefore, it appears that the insurance company has unjustifiably repudiated the claim of the plaintiff on the grounds of misrepresentation without verifying the complete and actual facts of the case and without following the Rules.
57. As noted above, a mere delay of 2 days was not sufficient to deny the claim to the plaintiff.
58. It is argued by Ld counsel for defendant no.1 that the reputation letter is dated 16.07.2019 whereas the plaintiff sent a letter dated 04.07.2019 mentioning that his claim had been repudiated.
It is stated that even before the receipt of the repudiation letter, the plaintiff knew that his claim would be repudiated.
59. I find no force in this argument.

The plaintiff has clearly stated in the plaint that the surveyor had told him that his claim was being repudiated after examining the vehicle on 15.06.2019 itself,
which fact is not disputed by defendant no.1.

Therefore, the repudiation was no secret even as on 04.07.2019.
60.

In these circumstances, I hold that defendant no.1 has failed to prove that the claim of the plaintiff was not maintainable due to misrepresentation of facts, non-disclosure of material information or due to delay in reporting.
Thus, the repudiation letter dated 16.07.2019 is liable to be struck down.
These issues are decided in favour of the plaintiff and against the defendants.

however, defendant no.1 did not put any suggestion to PW3 that the charges levied by him were excessive or that the repairs as reflected in Ex PW1/9 were not warranted due to the accident.
66. Ld counsel for defendant no.1 has argued that PW3 signed the invoice as a Partner of the workshop, whereas he was not a partner but only an employee.
It is thus argued that the testimony of PW3 is not reliable.
67. I have carefully perused the invoice.
Although the stamp on the invoice mentions the word "Partner" but the end of the bill mentions "Authorised Signatory."
68. PW3 was the best person to explain why the stamp bears the word "Partner" but no question was put to him by defendant no.1 during his cross-examination.
Further, no suggestion was put to him that the invoice was a forged one or that the vehicle was not so repaired.

"Issue no. ii) Whether the plaintiff is entitled for the relief of damages towards harassment, mental agony, etc, as prayed for? ...OPP"
76.
The onus of proving this issue was on the plaintiff.
The plaintiff is claiming 1,00,000 on account of damages for mental agony, 1,00,000 on account of expenditure incurred on cabs and other vehicles and 50,000 as loss of professional earnings.
77. The plaintiff has testified that he and his son Sh. Ashok Kumar/PW2 were using the vehicle for their work- related commitments.

It is stated that the plaintiff, who is a practising advocate, used to attend different courts in Delhi and also used to visit his native village at Mahindra Garh Haryana,
using the vehicle.

It is stated that Sh. Ashok Kumar was working in a company in Bahadurgarh,
Haryana and he also used the vehicle to go to his workplace.
It is stated that after the vehicle was damaged, they had no alternative but to use cabs.

78. PW2/Ashok Kumar has also testified that he used to attend his duty from Delhi to Bahadurgarh in the vehicle, and in the rainy season, he was constrained to avail services of Ola cab to reach his workplace.
79. Per contra, it is argued by Ld. Counsel for defendant no.1 that the accident was caused by PW2/the son of the plaintiff who did not have any insurable interest.

It is stated that the policyholder was the plaintiff and not his son and therefore, the damages claimed by the plaintiff on the expenses incurred by his son are not liable to be paid by the insurance company.
80.
I find merit in this contention.
It is only the plaintiff who had an insurable interest in the vehicle and he was the beneficiary under the insurance contract.
Therefore, the plaintiff can only claim losses suffered by him personally.
81. The accident took place on 13.06.2019.
After the insurance company refused to pass the claim of the plaintiff, he sent several correspondences to the company and finally, he got the vehicle repaired at his expense on 07.10.2019.
Thus, the plaintiff was unable to use the vehicle for about 3.5 months after the accident.
It is evident that due to this, the plaintiff suffered a significant inconvenience and financial burden.
During this period of approximately 3.5 months, the plaintiff had to rely on alternative transportation, such as cabs, which incurred additional expenses.

82. To compensate the plaintiff fairly, the insurance company should not only reimburse the plaintiff for the cost of the cab rides during the period when he was unable to use the vehicle but also for the inconvenience caused to him during this period.

sentences.text: An insurer procures insurance coverage with the expectation of recourse in the event of an unforeseen incident.
If the insurance company denies his claim arbitrarily, disregarding the Rules, it constitutes a severe lapse in service.
The rejection of claims in such a manner erodes the confidence of policy-holders in the insurance industry.
84. The plaintiff is a resident of Uttam Nagar, which is roughly 5-6 km from Dwarka Courts, which is the nearest court complex to his residence.
The plaintiff is a practising advocate and there is no reason to doubt him when he deposed that he was attending several courts in Delhi.

85. Accordingly, the expenses suffered by the plaintiff on account of hiring cabs are ascertained at 50,000.
86.
Further, defendant no.1 is also liable to pay compensation for mental agony resulting from its wrongful refusal of the claim and the subsequent delay in repairing the vehicle.
87. The plaintiff is a senior citizen.
He has testified how he kept pursuing with the surveyor/defendant no.1 but his calls would be disconnected.
The plaintiff has deposed that wrote correspondences to defendant no.1 and also IRDA but to no avail.

88. The prolonged period of uncertainty, frustration, and financial strain caused by defendant no.1's actions can be reasonably presumed to have had a significant impact on the plaintiff's mental well-being.
89. Even under conservative assessment, the plaintiff should be entitled to compensation amounting to 75,000.
90. However, since the plaintiff has not shown how and what loss was caused to him under the head "loss of professional earnings", no compensation is granted on that account.
91. Therefore, the plaintiff is entitled to recover 1,25,000 from defendant no.1 on account of damages.

This issue is decided in favour of the plaintiff and against defendant no.1.

92.

The plaintiff has claimed interest at the rate of 18% p.a. from the date of the accident and at the rate of 12% p.a. as pendente lite and future interest but no justification has been given for such exorbitant rates of interest.
93. Keeping in view the prevalent rates of interest and Section 34 CPC, interest at the rate of 6% per annum appears to be fair and just.

However, this condition should not prevent settlement of genuine claims, particularly when there is delay in intimation or in submission of documents due to unavoidable circumstances.
The insurer's decision to reject a claim shall be based on sound logic and valid grounds.
One needs to see the merits and good spirit of the clause, without compromising on bad claims.
Rejection of claims on purely technical grounds in a mechanical fashion will result in policyholders losing confidence in the insurance industry, giving rise to excessive litigation.
The Authority, vide circular no. IRDA/HLTH/MISC/ CIR/216/09/2011 dated 20.09.2011, issued guidelines as to how to deal with delayed intimation of claims and delayed submission of documents by the claimants.

the Authority further issued directions under section 34(1) of the Insurance Act, 1938 , vide no.IRDA/NL/MISC/CIR/214/10/2016 dated 28.10.2016 clarifying that the circular dated 20.09.2011 is binding on the insurers.
